article_units.name: Physical Factors Affecting Performance
article_units.subtitle: Applied anatomy and physiology, movement analysis, fitness, training and injury prevention.

lessons.title: The Skeletal System: Bones and Functions
lessons.description: Major bones, the six functions of the skeleton and how the skeleton supports physical activity.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR adds the 'posture' function explicitly (AQA bundled it with support) and includes carpals/metacarpals/phalanges/tarsals/metatarsals which AQA omitted. Re-spec to 1.1.a, expand the bone list to OCR's 19 bones, and add posture as a distinct function.

lessons.title: Synovial Joints and Movement at Joints
lessons.description: Hinge and ball-and-socket joints, articulating bones and the types of movement they allow.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR specifies the four named joints (knee, elbow, shoulder, hip) with articulating bones — AQA was less prescriptive. OCR omits plantar/dorsiflexion. Drop those movement types and re-spec to 1.1.a; emphasise articulating bones for each joint.

lessons.title: Muscles and Antagonistic Pairs
lessons.description: Major muscle groups, agonist, antagonist and fixator roles in antagonistic muscle action.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR adds trapezius, latissimus dorsi, pectorals, abdominals and gluteals — a wider muscle list than AQA — and explicitly includes 'fixator' as a third muscle role. Drop AQA's isotonic/isometric and concentric/eccentric content (OCR doesn't require it) and add fixator + the extra muscles.

lessons.title: Lever Systems in Sport
lessons.description: First, second and third class levers in the body and the meaning of mechanical advantage.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR pins each lever class to a specific body example (1st = neck, 2nd = ankle, 3rd = elbow). OCR only requires the definition of mechanical advantage, not the calculation method AQA tests. Strip the MA = effort arm/load arm calculation worked example and replace with the spec's three named body locations.

lessons.title: Planes and Axes of Movement
lessons.description: Frontal, transverse and sagittal planes and frontal, transverse and longitudinal axes in sporting actions.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR's named axes are frontal, transverse and longitudinal (NOT sagittal) — opposite to AQA's frontal/transverse/sagittal axis trio. Replace 'sagittal axis' with 'frontal axis' throughout. Planes are identical across boards.

lessons.title: The Cardiovascular System and Pathway of Blood
lessons.description: Heart structure, pulmonary and systemic circulation, blood vessels and key cardiac definitions.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR explicitly names the bicuspid/tricuspid/semilunar valves and the double-circulatory system (systemic vs pulmonary) — terminology AQA does not require. OCR also requires the role of red blood cells. Add these and drop AQA's vasoconstriction/vasodilation depth (not in OCR spec).

lessons.title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
lessons.description: Pathway of air, the role of respiratory muscles and gas exchange at the alveoli.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Near-identical content. OCR adds 'mouth' and 'nose' to the air pathway and uses 'breathing rate' rather than 'respiratory rate'. Re-spec to 1.1.d and tweak terminology.

lessons.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Exercise
lessons.description: Defining aerobic and anaerobic exercise and applying examples by intensity and duration.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR drops AQA's deeper content on EPOC, oxygen debt, DOMS and recovery methods (ice baths, massage, rehydration) — these belong to the AQA 8582 spec but not OCR J587. Strip the recovery-methods section and tighten the lesson to definition + intensity-and-duration justification only. Recovery is not assessed at this depth.

lessons.title: Short and Long Term Effects of Exercise
lessons.description: Immediate physiological responses and the long-term training adaptations of the body systems.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR's long-term effects list is broader and more granular: includes capillarisation, resting stroke volume, hypertrophy of the heart, resistance to fatigue and respiratory muscles by name. Add these named adaptations. Add 'redistribution of blood flow during exercise' to the short-term effects (OCR-specific). Bake in a data-collection prompt — OCR flags this topic for use of data.

lessons.title: Components of Fitness and Fitness Tests
lessons.description: The ten components of fitness, definitions and the standard tests used to measure each.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR groups definitions of fitness components and their tests into one combined topic (1.2.a), where AQA splits these across L10 and L11. Merge AQA's L10 component definitions with the test procedures. OCR adds the Cooper 12-minute run and press-up/sit-up tests; drop AQA's 'health vs fitness' definitional debate (AQA 3.1.3.1 only).

lessons.title: Principles of Training and FITT
lessons.description: Specificity, overload, progression, reversibility and the FITT principle applied to training programmes.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR uses SPOR (Specificity, Progression, Overload, Reversibility) — no 'tedium' principle, unlike AQA's SPORT. Drop tedium. Otherwise content is essentially identical.

lessons.title: Methods of Training
lessons.description: Continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight, plyometric and HIIT training methods matched to fitness aims.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Content list is essentially identical to AQA's L13. OCR explicitly names HIIT as a separate method; AQA folds it into interval. Drop AQA's 'static stretching' as a training method (not in OCR spec); keep all 7 named methods.

lessons.title: Warm Up and Cool Down
lessons.description: Components of a warm up, components of a cool down and the physical benefits of each.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR is more prescriptive about warm-up components (pulse raising, mobility, stretching, dynamic movements, skill rehearsal) — five named stages — and lists 8 specific physical benefits. Restructure around OCR's named lists. Drop AQA's 'mental preparation' framing (covered separately under sports psychology in OCR).

lessons.title: Preventing Injury in Physical Activity
lessons.description: Strategies that minimise injury risk and the hazards present in different sport and activity settings.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR-only topic. AQA has injury prevention scattered through L14 'Optimising Training and Preventing Injury' but does not assess hazards-by-setting or PPE-and-clothing as a distinct topic. OCR 1.2.c is its own learning outcome with explicit named settings (sports hall, fitness centre, playing field, artificial outdoor areas, swimming pool). Build fresh from spec.

article_units.name: Socio-Cultural Issues and Sports Psychology
article_units.subtitle: Engagement, commercialisation, ethics, sports psychology and the role of physical activity in wellbeing.

lessons.title: Engagement Patterns in Physical Activity and Sport
lessons.description: Current participation trends and the factors that affect engagement across different social groups.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR's factor list is broader than AQA's: explicitly includes time/work commitments, cost/disposable income, opportunity/access, environment/climate, media coverage, role models — and three named promotion strategies (promotion, provision, access). OCR also expects students to reference Sport England, NGBs and DCMS as data sources. Restructure the lesson around OCR's expanded list and the three-pronged participation-improvement strategy.

lessons.title: Commercialisation, Sponsorship and the Media
lessons.description: The golden triangle of sport and the positive and negative impacts of media and sponsorship.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR explicitly names four media types (social, internet, TV/visual, newspapers/magazines) — adapt AQA's L9 content to use this taxonomy. Drop the 'technology in sport' L10 content from AQA — OCR rolls technology into commercialisation/media rather than as a discrete topic.

lessons.title: Ethics in Sport: Sportsmanship, Gamesmanship and Deviance
lessons.description: The value of sportsmanship and the reasons performers turn to gamesmanship or deviance.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR uses the term 'deviance' (not in AQA's spec) and does not require AQA's 'contract to compete' phrase. Add the deviance definition with reasons (gain unfair advantage, peer pressure, win-at-all-costs culture). Drop 'contract to compete' framing.

lessons.title: Drugs in Sport
lessons.description: Why performers use drugs, the named PED categories and the impact of drug use on sport and performers.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR names only three PED categories (anabolic steroids, beta blockers, stimulants) — much narrower than AQA's six. Cut the AQA list to just these three. OCR also has no 'blood doping' content. Strip blood doping and EPO entirely. Add OCR's 'reasons performers use drugs' and 'impact on performers / impact on sport' framing — OCR-specific.

lessons.title: Violence in Sport
lessons.description: The reasons for player violence and how violence affects performers, officials and sport.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR-specific topic at this depth. AQA has 'spectator violence/hooliganism' but not 'player violence' as a distinct learning outcome. Build fresh from spec — focus on reasons (frustration, retaliation, intimidation, rivalry, alcohol/drugs, officiating decisions, win-at-all-costs culture) and practical examples from named sports.

lessons.title: Characteristics and Classification of Skill
lessons.description: Motor skills, the characteristics of skilful movement and the difficulty and environmental skill continua.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR uses only TWO continua (simple-complex, open-closed) where AQA uses FOUR (also self-paced/externally-paced and gross/fine). OCR also requires the five 'characteristics of skilful movement' (efficiency, pre-determined, co-ordinated, fluent, aesthetic) — AQA doesn't list these. Drop the two extra AQA continua and add OCR's characteristic-of-skill section. Drop AQA's 'skill vs ability' discussion (not in OCR spec).

lessons.title: Goal Setting and SMART Targets
lessons.description: Why we set goals in sport and how the SMART principle is applied to improve performance.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR's SMART acronym uses 'Achievable' and 'Recorded' — different from AQA's 'Accepted' and 'Realistic'. Replace those two letters in every SMART worked example. OCR also frames goal setting around adherence, motivation and performance (three named purposes). Drop AQA's 'performance vs outcome goals' distinction (not in OCR spec).

lessons.title: Mental Preparation Techniques
lessons.description: Imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking applied to sporting performance.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR teaches four discrete mental preparation techniques but does NOT cover arousal/inverted-U theory, optimal arousal or stress management as discrete content. Strip the inverted-U section from AQA L6. The four named techniques become the lesson's spine — give each a sporting worked example.

lessons.title: Types of Guidance in Sport
lessons.description: Visual, verbal, manual and mechanical guidance with their advantages and disadvantages.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Content list is identical (4 guidance types). OCR additionally requires advantages and disadvantages of each type with applied examples. Re-spec to 2.2 and pad the worked examples with explicit advantage/disadvantage tables for each guidance method.

lessons.title: Types of Feedback in Sport
lessons.description: Intrinsic, extrinsic, knowledge of performance, knowledge of results, positive and negative feedback.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Six named feedback types match AQA's almost exactly. Re-spec to 2.2 and tweak examples to OCR-favoured contexts. Worked examples should pair beginner-vs-elite scenarios.

lessons.title: Health, Fitness and Wellbeing
lessons.description: Defining health, fitness and wellbeing and the physical, emotional and social benefits of sport.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR places this in Paper 2 (component 02), where AQA placed it in the wellbeing block of Paper 2 too. OCR's named outcomes are more explicit: physical (CHD, BP, bone density, obesity, T2 diabetes, posture, fitness), emotional (self-esteem, stress management, image), social (friendship, belonging, loneliness). AQA was looser. Restructure around OCR's named lists; add age-group application as OCR explicitly tests 'apply to different age groups'.

lessons.title: Sedentary Lifestyle and Consequences
lessons.description: What a sedentary lifestyle is and how inactivity contributes to obesity, CHD, diabetes and poor wellbeing.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR does NOT include somatotypes (ectomorph/mesomorph/endomorph) — that's AQA-only. Strip somatotypes entirely and refocus on the spec's 'consequences of a sedentary lifestyle' learning outcome with the named conditions (obesity, CHD, T2 diabetes, hypertension, low self-esteem, loneliness). OCR also explicitly tests data response on health/fitness/wellbeing — bake in a data interpretation question.

lessons.title: Diet, Nutrition and Hydration
lessons.description: Components of a balanced diet, the role of macronutrients and the effect of hydration on performance.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR's seven named diet components (carbs, proteins, fats, minerals, vitamins, fibre, water/hydration) match AQA closely. Drop AQA's calorie-calculation depth (Kcal computations, daily energy need maths) — OCR only requires understanding of energy use, not calculation. Keep hydration and dehydration content.

unique_to_source.lesson: Using Data in Physical Activity and Sport (L16)
unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: OCR does not have a discrete 'use of data' lesson — data analysis is a cross-cutting requirement embedded within Applied Anatomy, Components of Fitness, Effects of Exercise and Health/Fitness/Wellbeing. Data interpretation is folded into existing OCR lessons rather than taught separately.

OCR splits this content: training optimisation is rolled into FITT/Methods of Training (no altitude training, heart rate zones or seasonal aspects in OCR spec), and injury prevention becomes the standalone OCR lesson 1.2.c with hazards-by-setting framing.
OCR does not include the input/decision-making/output/feedback information-processing model — it is AQA-specific (3.2.1.3).
OCR does not assess arousal or the inverted-U theory. OCR replaces this with the four mental preparation techniques only (imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention, positive thinking).
OCR does not assess personality types (introvert/extrovert), aggression types (direct/indirect) or motivation types (intrinsic/extrinsic) at GCSE — these are AQA-specific (3.2.1.5).
OCR rolls technology content into commercialisation/media (lesson 2 of unit 2). It is not a discrete OCR topic.
OCR replaces hooliganism with 'player violence' under 2.1.c — see new OCR lesson 5 in unit 2. Spectator hooliganism specifically is not a named OCR outcome.

unique_to_source.lesson: Interpreting Data on Participation and Performance (L17)
unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Same reason as the unit-1 data lesson — OCR treats data as a cross-cutting strand, not a standalone topic.

unique_to_target.why_no_source_match: OCR has injury prevention as a standalone learning outcome (1.2.c) with explicit hazards-by-setting and PPE-and-clothing strategies. AQA covers injury prevention only briefly inside its 'Optimising Training' lesson and does not assess hazards-by-setting.
OCR has 'reasons for player violence' as an explicit outcome under 2.1.c (Ethics) — AQA's nearest equivalent is spectator hooliganism, which is a different focus.

common_misconceptions.topic: Antagonistic muscle pairs and the role of the fixator
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students name a single muscle as 'the' agonist for a movement without specifying the joint, the direction of movement and which muscle is acting as antagonist. OCR additionally examines the role of the fixator, which AQA does not — students often omit this third role entirely. Content should always frame movement as agonist + antagonist + fixator anchored to a joint and a phase of movement (e.g. biceps agonist, triceps antagonist, deltoid fixator during the up phase of a bicep curl).
common_misconceptions.source: OCR teacher subject web page (https://www.ocr.org.uk/qualifications/gcse/physical-education-j587-from-2016/) and OCR J587 specification section 1.1.b

common_misconceptions.topic: Lever systems anchored to body locations
common_misconceptions.misconception: OCR pins each lever class to a specific body example (1st = neck, 2nd = ankle, 3rd = elbow). Students who memorise the order LFE without anchoring to OCR's three named body locations lose marks on the 'Identify the lever class operating at the ankle during plantar flexion' question type. Always teach lever class through the spec's three named body examples.

Students identify a sport as 'aerobic' or 'anaerobic' without justifying using duration and intensity. The OCR spec explicitly requires students to 'apply practical examples of aerobic and anaerobic activities in relation to intensity and duration' — justification is the marked content, not the label.

common_misconceptions.topic: Open vs closed skill placement on continua
common_misconceptions.misconception: OCR uses only TWO skill continua (simple-complex difficulty and open-closed environmental). Students confuse 'open' (environment changes) with 'simple' or 'gross' from other boards' continua. Reinforce that OCR only assesses the two continua and that students must justify placement on both — never one without the other.

OCR's 8-mark extended response items use levels-based marking and reward (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument, and (c) application to physical activity and sport. Students often produce one-sided answers or forget to apply each point to a named sporting context. Encourage 'On one hand... However...' structures with a sporting worked example anchored to each point.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR teacher support — assessment of extended response, J587 specification section 3h

common_misconceptions.misconception: OCR's SMART acronym is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded, Timed. Students who learn the more common 'Realistic' or 'Time-bound' variant (used by other boards) lose definition marks. Drill the OCR-specific letters from lesson 7 onwards and reinforce in flashcards.

student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Evaluate: OCR's top-tier extended response is 8 marks (not 9 like AQA). Students often produce one-sided arguments and forget to apply each point to a named sport. The mark scheme is levels-based and rewards (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument, and (c) sustained sporting application. Encourage 'For X... However Y...' paragraphs each anchored to a sporting example.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Analyse: Students list rather than analyse. Each point should be developed: state the factor, link it to performance, give a sporting example. Avoid bullet-point answers; encourage continuous prose.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Interpret Data: OCR explicitly tests data interpretation across both papers (use-of-data symbol marks the spec sections). Students copy numbers from the table without saying what they show. Always make a comparison, quote one figure, then explain the sporting implication.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Calculate from Data: Students forget the unit (e.g. bpm, %, seconds, l/min) or skip showing working. Mark schemes typically award one mark for working, one for the correct figure, one for the unit. Always show all three. Note: OCR allows a calculator on Paper 1.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — State Two: Students give two near-identical answers (e.g. 'increased heart rate' and 'heart rate goes up'). Mark schemes award once for the same physiological point — the second answer must be qualitatively different.

topic_weighting_notes: Component 01 (Physical factors affecting performance) is 30% of the qualification = 60 marks. Applied anatomy and physiology dominates this paper — every paper carries multi-mark questions on muscles, the cardio-respiratory system and the effects of exercise. Treat the first 9 lessons of unit 1 as the foundation block and revisit them in worked examples in later lessons (training, warm up, injury prevention).

Component 02 (Socio-cultural issues and sports psychology) is 30% of the qualification = 60 marks. Topics divide roughly equally between socio-cultural (engagement, commercialisation, ethics, drugs, violence) and sports psychology (skill, goals, mental preparation, guidance, feedback) plus the wellbeing strand. Allocate practice questions evenly across the two strands.

Use of data appears across both papers, marked in the OCR spec with the data-handling symbol. Bake data interpretation into practice questions throughout the build, not just into dedicated data lessons. Topics flagged for data: short-term and long-term effects of exercise, components of fitness, health/fitness/wellbeing, engagement patterns.

Socio-cultural and ethical issues (commercialisation, drugs, player violence) yield rich 6- and 8-mark questions. These lessons need contemporary, balanced examples with explicit positive and negative impacts framed.

Practical (Component 04) and Analysis & Evaluation (Component 05) together make up 40% of the qualification — 60 marks + 20 marks of NEA — but are teacher-assessed and not addressed by this revision platform. Students are pointed to their school's PE department for activity assessment and the analysis-and-evaluation coursework. The 27 lessons in this plan cover 100% of the assessable theory content for Components 01 and 02 (60% of the qualification).
current_spec_changes: OCR J587 specification version 1.7 (January 2024) is the current authoritative document. No content additions or removals affect the theory papers for the 2026 series. Source: https://www.ocr.org.uk/qualifications/gcse/physical-education-j587-from-2016/specification-at-a-glance/

OCR's NEA approved-activities list is updated periodically. Practical changes do not affect theory content. Refer to the OCR Guide to NEA in Physical Education for current approved activities. Source: https://www.ocr.org.uk/qualifications/gcse/physical-education-j587-from-2016/
pedagogical_notes: EEF guidance on retrieval practice: the active attempt to recall is what builds long-term memory; quizzes must include a delay between learning and recall, balance challenge with success, and provide feedback. Knowledge checks and flashcards in this build must be true retrieval tasks (not just re-reading) and should mix anatomy, training and socio-cultural content to force students to discriminate between related concepts. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-not-another-quiz-refining-retrieval-practice

EEF cognitive science review identifies dual coding (pairing words with diagrams) as a high-utility classroom strategy. PE content is anatomy-heavy: where a diagram would clarify (heart chambers, lever systems anchored to neck/ankle/elbow, planes/axes), the lesson should describe it precisely in text and include a key-fact 'sketch this without looking' retrieval prompt. Free-tier lessons do not embed generated images, so the prose must do the imaging work. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/evidence-reviews/cognitive-science-approaches-in-the-classroom

EEF spaced-practice principle: revisiting material across days outperforms massed practice. Lessons should explicitly cross-reference earlier lessons (e.g. when teaching warm-up, retrieve the cardio-respiratory and muscular adaptations from lessons 6 and 9). Build deliberate retrieval prompts into key-facts. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-putting-cognitive-science-principles-into-practice

EEF interleaving principle: mixing related topics in retrieval forces students to discriminate. Knowledge checks should not be pure single-topic — Component 01 lessons should mix anatomy with training, and Component 02 lessons should mix sports psychology with socio-cultural influences. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-the-abc-of-cognitive-science

Glossary terms: PE is terminology-dense (every named bone, muscle, joint, training method, principle and ethical concept needs precise definition). Aim for at least 6 inline glossary terms per lesson; 8–10 is realistic in anatomy lessons. Definitions should be one sentence and reusable across lessons.

Data interpretation: OCR Paper 1 and Paper 2 both test use of data. Generate ORIGINAL fictional data tables and graph descriptions in question stems — never reproduce real OCR figures. Use realistic numbers (e.g. 'Liam's heart rate during a 30-min run: rest 70 bpm, peak 165 bpm, recovery 90 bpm at 5 min'). Include at least one '4 marks — Interpret Data' or '3 marks — Calculate from Data' question in lessons where the topic is amenable (Cardiovascular System, Effects of Exercise, Components of Fitness, Engagement Patterns, Health/Fitness/Wellbeing, Diet and Nutrition). Source: OCR J587 specification, use-of-data symbol marking.

Mark scheme rubric: StudyVault uses Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging on 6- and 8-mark levels-based questions. NEVER use 'Level 1/2/3', 'Nothing worthy of credit' or 'Award X marks for Y'. Phrase mark allocations as '1 mark for X; 1 mark for Y' or 'Up to 3 marks: identification (1), context (1), explanation (1)'. The validator hard-bans the 'Award N marks for' pattern.

Plain-text fields (description, practice_questions[].text/.type/.marks, knowledge_checks[].q, flashcard_questions[].q/.a, glossary_terms[].term/.definition) MUST use plain unicode (apostrophes, en-dashes, em-dashes typed directly). NEVER use HTML entities such as ’, &, – in these fields — entities are only allowed inside content_html, exam_tip_html, conclusion_html.

Copyright: do not include spec codes (J587), paper codes (J587/01, J587/02), section labels, or OCR's trademark question stems verbatim. Do not write 'Other than X, identify...' style questions that mimic OCR's structure. Do not reproduce OCR mark scheme phrasing. Build generic GCSE-level questions with our 11 registered command-word types.

gaps: Practical NEA Component 04 (30% of qualification, 60 marks) is teacher-assessed and not addressed by this revision platform. Students are pointed to their school's PE department for the three approved practical activities (one team, one individual, one from either list).

Analysing and Evaluating Performance NEA Component 05 (10% of qualification, 20 marks) is teacher-assessed coursework completed under controlled conditions. Not covered by this platform. Students should refer to the OCR Guide to NEA in Physical Education and their teacher's notes.
The 27 lessons in this plan cover 100% of the assessable theory content for Components 01 and 02 (60% of the qualification, 120 marks total).
